Soldiers and Mariners Wills 161

According to the ancient English Law a disposition of either personal or real property could be made by an oral will. However, from the date of the Norman Conquest and the introduction of Feudalism into England in the year 1066 lands ceased to be devisable. By the Statute of 32 

Henry VIII, Chapter 1, lands were made devisable and it was provided that the devises should be in writing. The notorious perjury case involving an oral will of personalty known as Cole v. Mordaunt, see note in 4 Ves. 196, and also 

Prince v. Hazelton, 20 Johns. (N. Y.) 502, 11 Am. Dec. 307, gave rise to the Statute of Frauds, the appropriate provisions of which are as follows: "Statute of Frauds, 29 Car. II, c. 3, Section 18 (always cited as Section 19). "And for prevention of fraudulent practices in setting up nuncupative wills, which have been occasion of much perjury; be it enacted by the authority aforesaid, that from and after the aforesaid four and twentieth day of June, no nuncupative will shall be good where the estate thereby requested shall exceed the value of thirty pounds that is not proved by the oaths of three witnesses (at the least) that were present at the making thereof; nor unless it be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the same, did bid the persons present or some of them bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; nor unless such nuncupative will were made at the time of the last sickness of the deceased and in the 149

house of his or her habitation or dwelling, or where he or she hath been resident for the space of ten days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person was surprised or taken sick being from his own home, and died before he returned to the place of his or her dwelling." "Same, Section 19 (always cited as Section 20). "And be it further enacted that after six months passed after the speaking of the pretended testamentary words, no testimony shall be received to prove any will nuncupative, except the said testimony or the substance thereof were committed to writing within six days after the making of the said will." 

Same, Section 22 (always cited as Section 23). "Provided always, that notwithstanding this act, any soldier being in actual military service, or any mariner or seaman being at sea, may dispose of his moveables, wages, and personal estate as he or they might have done before the making of this act." 

See Rood on Wills, Sections 220, 221, 222 and Bigelow on 

Wills, page 63.

The corresponding provisions in our own statutes are found in Section 3 of the Act of 1705, 1 Sm. L. 33, and Section 

7 of the Wills Act of 1833. These earlier statutes are now supplanted by Section 4 of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 403, 20 P. S. Section 193, which reads as follows: 

"Personal estate may be bequeathed by a nuncupative will, under the following restrictions: (a) Such will shall in all cases be made during the last sickness of the testator, and in the house of his habitation or dwelling, or where he has resided for the space of ten days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person shall be surprised by sickness, being from his own house. (b) Where the sum or value bequeathed shall exceed one hundred dollars, it shall be proved that the testator, at the time of pronouncing the bequest, did bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect; and, in all cases, the foregoing requisites shall

NUNCUPATION 

151 be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making of such will. (c) No testimony shall be received to prove any nuncupative will after six months elapsed from the speaking of the alleged testamentary words, unless the said testimony, or the substance thereof, were committed to writing within six days after the making of said will."

A nuncupative will, therefore, at the present day represents a survival of an ancient general practice that wills of both personalty and realty were not required to be in writing. However, this survival now represents the exception to the general statutory rule that all wills, both of personalty and realty, must be in writing. 

Consequently, the specifications of a good nuncupation are numerous and stringent with the result that the books afford but few instances of valid nuncupations although there are many cases wherein the Courts have pointed out a failure to validly nuncupate owing to a lack of observance of one or more of the requirements.

These remarks are not applicable to the wills of mariners while at sea or soldiers while in actual military service. 

As has been noted already the Statute of Frauds specifically excepted these two classes of persons and those exceptions have come down through the Pennsylvania Statutes of 1705, 1833 and the present Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403, Section 

5 of which provides as follows: "Notwithstanding this act, any mariner being at sea, or any soldier being in actual military service, may dispose of his movables, wages, and personal estate, as he might have done before the making of this act." 

Excepting the classes just mentioned the requirements for nuncupation are set forth by Beaver, J. in Megary's 

Estate, 25 Pa. Super. Ct., 243 wherein it is said: "In order to the validity of a nuncupative will, as appears by the provisions of the Statute of April 8, 1833, P. L. 249, sec. 7, and the decisions of the Supreme Court relating thereto, seven distinct requisites must affirmatively appear and be clearly proved:

1. It must relate to personal property. 

2. It must be made during the last sickness of the testator and, as stated in Werkheiser v. Werkheiser, 6 W. & 

S. 184, and Taylor's Appeal, 47 Pa. 31, in such extremity thereof as precluded a written will. 

3. It must be made "in the house of (testator's) habitation or dwelling or where he has resided for the space of ten days or more next before the making of such will, except where such person shall be surprised by sickness, being from his own house, and shall die before returning thereto." 

4. "Where the sum or value bequeathed shall exceed one hundred dollars, it shall be proved that the testator at the time of pronouncing the bequest did bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will or to that effect." 

5. "In all cases the foregoing requisites shall be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making of such will.” 

6. The decedent must have intended to make a will which was to be a nuncupative one. 

As declared in Taylor's Appeal, 47 Pa. 31, the testimony relating to the said will or the substance thereof must be committed to writing within six days after the making of such will."

The above specifications will now be discussed in order of their statement.

PERSONAL PROPERTY 

It is specifically set forth in Section 4 of the Wills Act of 1917 already quoted that nuncupation is confined to a disposition of personal estate under certain conditions and in no case can a nuncupation be made of real estate. This same restriction is further evidenced in Section 20 (a) of the Wills Act of 1917 wherein it is stated that a will concerning real estate shall not be repealed or revoked except as set forth in the paragraph and on the other hand in paragraph (b) of this same section it is specified that a will concerning personal estate may be repealed or revoked by a nuncupation.

NUNCUPATION 

153 

Ann. Cas. 1912 C 646, Costigan's Cases on Wills, Second 

Edition 138, note, wherein authorities are cited showing that except in Georgia real estate seems not to pass under nuncupative wills though formerly it did in New Mexico and in Ohio. The reader is referred to the notes of the above volume pages 138 and 139 for interesting and valuable information. See also Weisner's Estate, 17 Berks 282.

LAST SICKNESS 

In Boyer v. Frick, 4 W. & S. 357, the decedent in expectation of an operation to be performed made a verbal disposition of her personalty before witnesses. The operation occurred soon thereafter and she survived the same two days. In reversing judgment for the plaintiffs who were the beneficiaries under the parol will Gibson, C. J. observed: "Nuncupation is not a matter of right, but, of special indulgence, as a last resource. It is an exception to the rule of the statute, which has no foundation but necessity, and which, as it affords great temptation to the perjury and fraud which it was the aim of the leading provisions to prevent, cannot be resorted to as a measure of mere convenience. It is true that the statute, speaking in general terms, allows it in the last sickness, without specifying the degree of its urgency; but from the clause which requires the act to be done 'in the house of the testator's habitation or dwelling, except where such person shall be surprised by sickness" abroad, we may safely infer that the compilers of the statute contemplated a state of illness so violent as to deprive the patient of power to comply with the general regulation. There could be no reason to license the making of a verbal statement in the last, rather than in any previous sickness, where the danger to be feared from misapprehension or corruption of the witness, might be avoided as readily in the one case as in the other. Why the compilers did not define the emergency which dispenses with the signature merely, in the very words they used to define the emergency which dispenses with writing altogether, it would be hard to conjecture, were it not for the fact that the words 'last sickness,' used in connection with the subject of nuncupa-

tion in the former statute also, had received a judicial construction in Yarnall's Will (4 Rawle 46), which it may have been thought impolitic to disturb." 

In Mellor v. Smyth, 220 Pa. at page 174, Mestrezat, J. declared: "In construing the language of our statute, we have adopted the views of Chancellor Kent in the leading American case of Prince v. Hazleton, 20 Johns 502, in construing a similar statute, in which he holds that a nuncupative will is not good, unless it be made by a testator when he is in extremis, or overtaken by sudden and violent sickness, and has not time or opportunity to make a written will; Priscilla 

Yarnall's Will, 4 Rawle, 46; Boyer v. Frick, 4 W. & S. 357;

Werkheiser v. Werkheiser, 6 W. & S. 184. If, therefore, a nuncupative will is presented for probate, one of the essential requisites of its validity which must be made to appear is that it was made in the last sickness of the testator and that by reason of the near approach of death there was neither time nor opportunity for the testator to execute a written will. The provisions of the statute are mandatory that a will must be in writing and signed by the testator, unless he is prevented from so doing by the immediate apprehension of death and there is neither time nor opportunity to make a written testament. There must be an urgent necessity or an emergency to justify a nuncupation."

For valuable note distinguishing the meaning of the phrase "last sickness" in cases of gifts causa mortis, claims under statutes giving preference to expenses incurred in the last sickness of a decedent and those of nuncupative wills, see 9 A. L. R. page 462.

In Wiley's Estate, 187 Pa. at page 87, Mitchell, J. observed: "The court below also held that the will was ineffectual because not made in the extremity of the decedent's last sickness. On this point we entertain some doubt. There are mental as well as physical elements in such matters, and one of the former is the hopefulness of invalids who are unwilling to believe that death is near. Therefore,

NUNCUPATION 

155 although there was sufficient time, even after the physician had warned the decedent to settle her affairs, for her to have made a will in writing, yet if she through misplaced confidence in her ability to "pull through," as the doctor expressed it, postponed doing so, it would not necessarily follow that she might not yet make a valid nuncupative will. But it is unnecessary to consider this point further, as the will clearly fails on the others." 

It is not believed that the quotation just made represents correctly the law in Pennsylvania. The leading cases confined the meaning of "last sickness" in nuncupative cases very narrowly. Consequently, if there is no imminence of death or a failure to realize the same or despite a serious and last sickness an opportunity to make a written will, the Courts have stated there is no valid nuncupation. See Rutt's 

Estate, 200 Pa. 549. 

Munhall's Estate, 234 Pa. 169.

For authority giving a more liberal view of the phrase "last sickness" than that adopted in Pennsylvania and other jurisdictions, see 10 Ann. Cas. 1128, and 14 Ann. Cas. 1162.

HABITATION, ETC. 

Paragraph a of Section 4 of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 

403, provides not only that the nuncupation must be during the last sickness of the testator but in addition thereto the nuncupation must take place "in the house of his habitation or dwelling, or where he has resided for the space of ten days or more, next, before the making of such will." 

In other words besides last sickness there must be the designated place which must be his habitation or dwelling or in the alternative where he has resided for the space of ten days or more. There follows in the paragraph an exception "where such person shall be surprised by sickness, being from his own house." Rood on Wills, Second

Edition, Section 235, observes: 

"Oral wills of others than soldiers and sailors must still be made at the home of the deceased, unless he was taken sick while away, in Alabama, Arkansas, Georgia, Maine,

Missouri, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Texas, Washington and Wisconsin."

ROGATIO TESTIUM 

In the leading case of Yarnall's Will, 4 Rawle at page 

62, Rogers, J. explains: "It must be observed, that there is a marked difference, as regards the attestation, between a written and a nuncupative will, the legislature having placed many guards on the latter, which were unnecessary on the former. A written will may be reduced to writing at one time, and attested by the witnesses at different times. Not so as we conceive in the case of a nuncupative will, which more nearly resembles the formula observed in the civil law. 

In the Roman jurisprudence it was held, that a testament ought to be made uno contextu, without any foreign act intervening, and the witnesses were likewise required to attest without separating, or even discontinuing the act of subscribing, till all was complete. The legislature, in the 

Act of 1705, evidently looked to the nuncupative, as an evil, and it will not do for the testator to declare his will first in the presence of one witness, and afterwards in the presence of another witness, as in the Roman law, it does not seem that the witnesses were even released from the necessity of subscribing at one time, and in each other's presence, so we think that the requisite number of witnesses must be present, and called on to attest at the same time, of the alleged nuncupation. The act says, the will must be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making thereof. We are further of the opinion, that the rogatio testium, the calling on persons to bear witness to the act, must also be done at the time of the nuncupation, and that this must be proved by two or more witnesses, who were present at the time. I cannot conceive why inferior proof should suffice. It is an important part of the nuncupation, and goes far to show the animus testandi of the deceased, and for this purpose it was that the act requires that the testator should call on the witnesses to

NUNCUPATION 

157 remember that such was his will. The act says, the will shall not be good unless the testator, at the time of pronouncing the same, did bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will, or to that effect. 

The legislature go upon the supposition, that more than two may be present, who may be called on to bear witness to the publication of his will, or that the testator may bid some of them, (not some one of them,) to bear witness that such is his will. We think this construction necessary, as a guard against fraud, to which nuncupations are particularly exposed. I cheerfully admit, that the act does not require any particular words for a rogatio testium. It is certainly sufficient if the Court is satisfied, that the deceased meant to do a testamentary act, and wished the persons to attest, but I cannot agree, that if he desired only one to attest it, that satisfies the requisition of the statute. 

Still less can I suppose, that the rogatio testium to different witnesses at different times, would fulfill its requirements." 

The requirement of calling upon the witnesses is further explained by Mitchell, J. in Wiley's Estate, 187 Pa. at page 86: "There must not only be the testator's intent to make a will then and there, but an explicit call on persons present to bear witness that such was the intended effect of the testator's declaration. The words of the statute are that "it shall be proved that the testator at the time of pronouncing the bequest did bid the persons present, or some of them, to bear witness that such was his will or to that effect:" Act of April 8, 1833, sec. 7, P. L. 249. The phrase "or to that effect" was intended to prevent the inference that any set form of words should be necessary, but not to diminish the requirement of a distinct and explicit request by the testator to persons present to remember and be ready to testify that the testator was thereby making his will. "The rogatio testium, the calling on persons to bear witness to the act, must also be done at the time of the nuncupation, and must be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the time:" Yarnall's Will, 4 Rawle 46, 63. There

is an entire absence of affirmative evidence that the decedent in this case bade the persons who testified to bear witness that what she was saying was her will, or that she used any expression which, even by liberal construction, can be treated as a request "to that effect." She did desire the presence of the family, but even that is only proved by one witness, the nurse, and the purpose was not stated." 

To the same effect see Rutt's Estate, 200 Pa. 549.

For an interesting note on the doctrine of rogatio testium see 10 Ann. Cas. 1132. 

Meisenhelter's Will, 15 Phila. 651.

As has been noted in Section 4, paragraph b of the Wills Act of 1917, the rogatio testium only applies "where the sum or value bequeathed shall exceed one hundred dollars." 

Up to and including the sum of one hundred dollars, the provisions of paragraph b of Section 4 are applicable, as to the two witnesses.

WITNESSES Paragraph b of Section 4 of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 

403, 20 P. S. Section 193, provides, inter alia, that "in all cases, the foregoing requisite shall be proved by two or more witnesses who were present at the making of such will."

In determining the matter of proof under the similar provision in the Wills Act of 1833, it was said by Lowrie, J. in 

Haus v. Palmer, 21 Pa. 296: "The evidence of a verbal will is part of its very essence. 

The law makes it so, when it requires that some persons present shall be called upon by the testator to bear witness that such is his will, and that two of them must prove it. 

When the law requires persons to bear witness, it means that they shall be competent as witnesses. We make it speak nonsense, if we make it mean that the parties shall bear witness, a phraseology which, even in common parlance, is not free from absurdity. It is of great importance that there should be disinterested persons present at the making of such wills, and the law intended to provide for

NUNCUPATION 

159 

this. It may be that the rule sometimes defeats verbal wills. But what of that? People often die unintentionally intestate; but the general rule is too valuable to be endangered by accommodating it to isolated cases of hardship." "The general rule requiring all wills to be in writing, is intended to be as nearly universal as is possible, and the exception in favor of nuncupative wills must be very strictly administered. It is a partial substitute for a written will in cases of necessity. A necessity not arising from ignorance; for, besides the difficulty of proving or disproving ignorance, it is plain that the form of the exception is expected to be known, in order to be followed. A necessity not arising from mere carelessness, for that would be an abuse of the term. The necessity intended is that which arises when the testator is surprised by approaching death, and has not time to make the form of disposition intended by the general rule of law." Accord, Yarnall's Appeal, 4 Rawle 46. 

Rutt's Estate, 200 Pa. 549.

NUNCUPATIVE INTENT 

In order to have a valid nuncupation, in addition to the requisites already discussed, it must appear that there was on the part of testator, an intent to nuncupate. In Porter's 

Appeal, 10 Pa. at page 260, Coulter, J. remarked: "The statute obviously meant that the intent to nuncupate should exist. After providing that all wills shall be in writing, there is, by way of proviso, a provision to make a nuncupative will of personal estate, under certain restrictions; that is, a decedent shall be allowed, in extremes, to dispose of his personal estate, where he intends to do that, and had not time to make or complete a written will. 

For the whole scope and policy of the law is, that when there is time, the will must be written; but when there is not time, a verbal disposition of the personal estate alone is allowed in extremity. But, no word was spoken by the

decedent of a nuncupative will. The completion of the written memorandum was not prevented by the act of God, but by the wilfulness or ignorance of man. There was abundant time, after the memorandum was written, to have signed it, if testator was able, and there is no evidence that he was not; or if so, the time was full of opportunity for the scrivener to write it for him." 

To the same effect, Wiley's Estate, 187 Pa. 82. 

Rutt's Estate, 200 Pa. 549. 

Megary's Estate, 25 Pa. Super. Ct. 243. 

Glebus's Estate, 267 Pa. 125. 

See also Shover's Estate, 258 Pa. 70, wherein the probate of an alleged nuncupative will was properly set aside where it appeared that the testatrix could for a period of at least thirty six hours after the making of the alleged will, have made a written will but that she made no effort to do so although she fully realized the serious nature of her illness. Satar's Estate, 275 Pa. 420. 

See also

PROOF 

Taylor's Appeal, 47 Pa. 31 and 54 A. L. R. 918. 

Ann. Cas., 1917 D. 608, Note. 

Fouche's Estate, 147 Pa. 395.

Paragraph c of Section 4 of the Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 

403, provides that "no testimony shall be received to prove any nuncupative will after six months elapsed from the speaking of the alleged testamentary words, unless the said testimony or the substance thereof, were committed to writing within six days after the making of said will." 

In Taylor's Appeal, 47 Pa. at page 36, Thompson, J. declared: "Wills of this description are not favorites of the law, and are only allowed in the extremity of the testator's last sickness, and when it has been so sudden, unexpected, and violent as to prevent him from putting his testamentary

NUNCUPATION 

161 wishes into writing (6 W. & S. 188), all the requisites of the law for the establishment of such wills must be strictly complied with: 4 Rawle 46. One of them is, that the testimony, or the substance thereof, must be committed to writing within six days after the making of such will. 

Neither the words nor the substance of them, as used by the alleged testator, were ever committed to writing in this case as proof of a bequest, or to be preserved as such by any one." 

See also Rutt's Estate, 200 Pa. 549.

The effect of the stipulations of paragraph c is to preclude any proof of a nuncupative will after the period of six months from the speaking of the alleged testamentary words unless the same or the substance thereof was reduced to writing within the period of six days after the making of said will. Conversely, if the testimony has been so reduced then it can be admitted at any future time. 

For the cognate subject of donations causa mortis, see the following cases: 

Nicholas v. Adams, 2 Wharton 17.

Headley v. Kirby, 18 Pa. 326. 

Michener v. Dale, 23 Pa. 59. 

Linsenbigler v. Gourley, 56 Pa. 166. 

Gourley v. Linsenbigler, 51 Pa. 345. 

Trough's Estate, 75 Pa. 115. 

Williams's Appeal, 106 Pa. 116. 

Appeal of Waynesburg College, 111 Pa. 130. 

Walsh's Appeal, 122 Pa. 177. 

Packer v. Clemson, 269 Pa. 4.

SOLDIERS AND MARINERS WILLS Section 5 of the Wills Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 403, 20 

P. S. Section 193, provides in substance, that "any mariner being at sea or any soldier being in actual military service" shall be exempt from the requirements heretofore discussed in the matter of will making so far as "his movables, wages and personal estate" are concerned. 

In Henninger's Estate, 30 D. R. 413, the parol will of a

soldier nineteen years of age killed in France during the World War was offered for probate before the Register of Wills in the County of Philadelphia. While being carried back from the front the soldier said: "Sergeant, if you get back alright, tell Mrs. T. that she can have everything I have and all my stuff." This declaration was proved by the testimony of the Sergeant and one of the stretcher bearers and was held by Gest, J. to be a good nuncupative will. 

It was further held that the wills of mariners at sea and soldiers in actual military service are not subject to the provisions of the Wills Act of 1705, 1 Smith Laws 33, April 

8, 1833, P. L. 249, and June 7, 1917, P. L. 403, being excepted from the operation of these statutes and are consequently, governed by the common law under which a will of personal property by word of mouth was valid made by a boy over fourteen years of age although a minor.

This case contains a most illuminating discussion of the general subject and a complete review of the authorities in England and in this and other states.

Form Intent CHAPTER VIII  PAGE PAGE 164 Extrinsic Evidence of Testa- 

164 mentary Intent

Discussion 

174 178 The Wills Act of 1917, as well as the preceding statutes of 1705 and 1833, specifies neither the form nor the materials to be used in the preparation of a will. 

The Wills Act provides that every will shall be in writing but there is no special provision as to the material with which or upon which a will may be written. As in the case of signing which, as we have heretofore observed, was, according to the construction of the Courts left to the customs of the people and to the times in which the law was operating, so in the case of materials to be used. Ancient wills were written upon parchment and in very early times sheets of wax were written upon, and in still earlier times clay tablets were used. To-day paper is the ordinary means and the characters upon the paper may be written either in ink or in pencil. It was formerly questioned as to whether a will written in lead pencil was good, and in Myers v. Vanderbelt, 84 Pa. 510 (1877), this matter was set at rest by our Supreme Court holding distinctly that a will written and signed with lead pencil, "in writing" within the meaning of the Wills Act, and is therefore valid. 

In Woodward's Will, 1 W. N. C. 177, there was a will written upon a slate with a slate pencil but the validity did not come directly before the court and hence the question was not determined. However the general deduction from the case and the reasoning thereof appears to be that any material whatsoever may be used, provided it disclosed a testamentary intent. In the case of perishable 163

materials it may be argued that the writing was deliberative and not final, and hence lacking in testamentary intent and in the case of wills written upon slates it may appear that the matter was not seriously considered but perpetrated simply as a joke or as an experiment. If the seriousness of the matter is clearly disclosed, there is no reason in the law why such a will should not be probative. Accord, Tomlinson's Estate, 133 Pa. 245. 

Smith v. Beales, 33 Pa. Super. Ct. 570. 

Flanders v. Snare, 37 Pa. Super. Ct. at page 31.

For note on the subject of signing various legal papers in lead pencil see 8 A. L. R. 1339, Note.

FORM 

In Kimmel's Estate 278 Pa. 435, Simpson, J. said: "While the informal character of a paper is an element in determining whether or not it was intended to be testamentary (Kisecker's Est., 190 Pa. 476), this becomes a matter of no moment when it appears thereby that the decedent's purpose was to make a posthumous gift. On this point the 

Court below well said: "Deeds, mortgages, letters, powers of attorney, agreements, checks, notes etc., have all been held to be in legal effect wills. Hence, an assignment (Coulter v. Shelmadine, 204 Pa. 120), a deed (Turner v. Scott, 51 Pa. 126), a letter of instructions (Scott's Est., 147 Pa. 89), a power of attorney (Rose v. Quick, 30 Pa. 225), and an informal letter of requests (Knox's Est., 131 Pa. 220), were all held as wills." 

See Bingaman's Estate, 281 Pa. at page 506.

INTENT 

Whatever is the form of the paper alleged to be a will it must be proved to have been made with testamentary intent.

In Stein v. North, 3 Yeates 324, it was held that a letter written by an uncle to his nephew promising that if the

nephew would come to this country and prove obedient and follow his directions, that he, the uncle, would make the nephew heir of his whole estate, was not precise enough to operate either as a will or as a contract.

In Shields v. Irwin, 3 Yeates, 389 the facts were that 

Thomas Mifflin executed an instrument under seal declaring that he was justly indebted to a certain person for personal services and that his executors should pay to this person the sum of $1,000. This instrument was held to be an obligation and not a testamentary disposition. 

Another early case disclosing facts indicative of a debt rather than a will is found in Toner v. Taggart, 5 Binney 490. 

See also Plumstead's App., 4 S. & R. 545.

In Rose v. Quick, 30 Pa. 225, a paper was in the form of a power of attorney authorizing two persons therein named to administer on the subscriber's estate and to make certain disposition of the property of the subscriber. This was held to be a good will and the persons therein named although not specifically described as executors, nevertheless, were such and by the terms of the paper empowered to sell the real estate of the testator. 

In Patterson v. English, 71 Pa. 545, there was a feigned issue directed by the Register of Wills to determine the validity of a paper purporting to be the will of the decedent. 

This paper consisted of six different items written with a lead pencil on the last four pages of the decedent's memo randum book entitled "Merchants Account Book and 

Buyer's Guide," which was found in a drawer in the desk of the decedent. The items were wholly disconnected and separated from each other by spaces of greater or less width and a line drawn between them with the name of C. E. Patterson written with a lead pencil immediately below the last item. It was held that this paper did not disclose any evidence of a testamentary disposition and should have been rejected as a will. In this case, Williams, J. questions whether a will written or signed with a lead pencil is valid on account of the facility with which the writing may be altered or effaced.

In Frew v. Clarke, 80 Pa. 170, the following was the paper offered for probate: "Know all men by these presents, that I, James McCully, of Pittsburgh, Pa., do hereby order and direct my administrators or executors, in case of my death, to pay Robert D. 

Clarke, the sum of $75,000, as a token of my regard for him, and to commemorate the long friendship existing between us. 

Witness my hand and seal this 17th day of April, A. D. 1872. $75,000. 

James McCully. (L.S.)."

It was held that the above writing signed at the end thereof possessed all the essential characteristics of a will and was undoubtedly testamentary in its character. 

Fosselman v. Elder, 98 Pa. 159. The testatrix executed a will in 1878 by which she bequeathed certain legacies to a niece, Isabella Fosselman. She later died suddenly and among her papers was found a sealed envelope endorsed in her handwriting as follows: "Dear Bella, this is for you to open." The envelope contained a promissory note for $2000.00 and the following paper was in testatrix's hand

"Lewistown, October 2nd 1879. My wish is for you to draw this $2000.00 for your use should I die sudden. Elizabeth Fosselman."

It was held that the endorsement on the envelope and the contents thereof together constituted a valid testamentary disposition of the note to the person named in the endorsement on the envelope, the combination operating as a codicil to the testatrix's will. 

See also Long's Appeal, 86 Pa. 196.

In Wilson v. VanLeer, 103 Pa. 600, the decedent executed and delivered to the plaintiff the following paper: 66 'August 13, 1865. I give thes fiew lines to Caroline Carman to show that I want her to have the sum of Twelve hundred dolars at my death she livd with mee A number of years And get verry little for it so i thought It rite to

leave her This little sum to be paid to her out of my home property. from Needham Wilson."

After Wilson's death Caroline brought assumpit against his executors, the claim being founded on the above paper and also on a count in quantum meruit. It was held that the above paper was testamentary in character and hence did not support an action in assumpsit. Further, the paper not having been admitted to probate was inadmissible in evidence under the general claim for services. 

In Turner v. Scott, 51 Pa. 126, a father executed "an indenture" to his son with general warranty for a tract of land in fee, in consideration of love and affection, performing certain services and maintaining grantor's wife if she survived him, reserving the land to the grantor for his life, the "conveyance in no way to take effect until after his decease." In an action of ejectment brought after the death of the father by certain of his devisees against the grantee in the above "indenture" it was held that the instrument in question was testamentary in character and therefore revocable and as the father had specifically revoked this instrument by a later will devising the property in question to the plaintiffs they were entitled to recover in this action. Said Woodward, J.: "The doctrine of the case is, that whatever the form of the instrument, if it vest no present interest but only appoints what is to be done after the death of the maker, it is a testamentary instrument. It signifies nothing that the parties meant to make a deed instead of a will. If they have used language which the law holds to be testamentary, their intention is to be gathered from the legal import of the words they have employed, for all parties must be judged by the legal meaning of their words." 

In Scott v. Scott, 70 Pa. 244, it was held, following the above case, that the writing in form of a deed, but in fact a will, which contained a covenant of warranty of land designed to be passed, was not a covenant of warranty in view of the fact that the instrument was a will and not

a deed. Furthermore, as the instrument granted real estate to the grantee after the death of the grantor and in the meantime the grantor devised the land in question to others, there could not be a breach of the covenant so as to subject the grantor or his executors after his death to an action. It was also observed to sustain an action on a covenant of warranty there must be an actual or constructive eviction by title paramount. 

In Schad's Appeal, 88 Pa. 111, the decedent after reciting the fact that he had insured his life in a certain insurance company assigned the proceeds of the policy to his wife. to take effect after his death, "when she can do with it according to her best will, without partiality toward her children. 

This I have written with good sound mind and set my name to it. Conrad Schad."

It was held that this paper was testamentary in character and that the wife as administratrix was bound to account for and was properly surcharged with the amount of the insurance.

A further case distinguishing Turner v. Scott is that of 

Book v. Book, 104 Pa. 240, wherein Jacob Book agreed to sell a certain tract of land to Michael H. Book. "The said 

Jacob Book to retain the possession and enjoyment of said land while he lives; he to use the premises in such reasonable manner so as not to deteriorate or depreciate their value and he to pay all taxes thereon while he so lives, and upon his death the said M. H. Book to have full and entire possession and enjoyment thereof."

In consideration of which the said M. H. Book covenanted to do certain things, inter alia, to build a dwelling house on the said premises or to repair the present house during the next year following the agreement and also to keep the premises in repair and at the death of Jacob Book to pay to certain persons specified sums of money. 

This instrument was held to be a contract inter vivos and not a will and therefore was not revoked by the subsequent will of Jacob Book who attempted to devise the same premises to his son, Aaron Book. The facts were that about MAMA

a year after the date of the above agreement, Michael H. 

Book was adjudged a bankrupt and at a sale of his assets the plaintiff in the present case purchased his interest in the land in dispute. This was an action of ejectment brought by the plaintiff against the heirs at law of the deceased devisee, Aaron Book. Said Sterrett, J.: "It is not necessary that a contract for the sale of real estate should vest in the vendee a right of immediate and exclusive possession. It is enough if it creates, as the contract in this case did, a vested interest to be enjoyed in possession, in futuro." 

In Bowlby v. Thunder, 105 Pa. 173, the testator left a will properly signed and in usual legal form giving his entire estate to his wife. Certain memoranda containing admonitions from the testator as to what the beneficiary under his will should do were offered in probate along with the will proper. It was held that these two papers although admitted to probate form no part of the testator's will and did not create a trust or in any way qualify the estate given to the wife.

In Sullivan's Estate, 130 Pa. 342, the paper, written upon a leaf of a memorandum book was in this form: "March the 4 Will my properti to my wief my death John Sullivan."

It was held that this paper was properly admitted by the 

Register as a will.

In Knox's Estate, 131 Pa. 220, the paper offered for probate consisted of three of the four pages of an ordinary folded sheet of letter paper written with a lead pencil and in the form of a letter, not, however, addressed to any one in particular. The writer outlined a number of things that she wanted done and also designated who were to have certain articles of wearing apparel and also certain moneys. The only language in the paper indicating testamentary intent was this sentence: "Please have just my baptismal names on stones, daughter of E. J. and Felician 

Slataper." It was held, per Mitchell, J., that the writing in question was "clearly testamentary," as it had the essential element of being a disposition of property to take effect after death.

In Lines v. Lines, 142 Pa. 149, it was held that a voluntary deed transferring property to a trustee to be distributed by him among specified beneficiaries at such time as in his discretion he should see proper, the income to be paid to the donor during life till the distribution, but not made before his death, with a power of revocation reserved to the donor, is not a testamentary instrument. Furthermore, such a deed involving personal property can not be impeached by the wife as in fraud of her rights, nor can it be said that a reserved right of revocation is inconsistent with the creation of a valid trust. 

In Scott's Estate, 147 Pa. 89, the decedent in his last illness had a paper presented in the form of a letter to his attorney giving him instructions relative to the preparation of a will. This paper was executed by the decedent and handed to the scrivener who signed it as a witness. After the paper was signed and delivered to the scrivener a son of the decedent came into the room with whom the decedent had previously discussed the subject of his will. In the presence of the scrivener the decedent told his son he had then signed his will. The paper in question was offered for probate and the signature was proved by three witnesses. 

It was held that parol evidence of the declarations of the decedent to the scrivener and the son were admissible to prove the publication of the paper though it was in the form of a letter of instruction, and further, that though the son did not see the paper when the declarations as to its publication were made, yet the circumstances, his connection and familiarity with the entire transaction, pointing directly to the immediate act of disposition made his testimony directly admissible and with that of the scrivener a sufficient compliance with the statute. 

In Sunday's Estate, 167 Pa. 30, the facts were that the testator thirteen years after he made his will executed seven judgment notes payable to his children and grandchildren. 

The notes were drawn and witnessed by a justice of the peace. Decedent requested the justice to keep the notes until he called for them and in case he should not call for them after the death of the maker, the justice should

deliver them to the parties named. The decedent never called and after his death the justice delivered the notes as instructed. It was testified by one of the daughters of the decedent that he had said to her that "he had made out papers so that it would cover all his personal property after his death to go to his children." It was held in an appeal from the decision of the Register of Wills refusing probate of these notes as codicils to the will of the testator, that the evidence was not sufficient to establish the testamentary character of the notes and their probate was properly refused. It

In Gaston's Estate, 188 Pa. 374, the writing in lead pencil was on the back of a printed gas notice and was found after the death of the decedent in a bureau drawer. The language was to the effect that certain persons were to have certain real and personal property but not indicating when or stating directly that the paper was a will. began with these words: "it my wish" and concluded with a statement that a certain person was to "keep the blance." 

It was held that this paper having been properly signed was a will and that it was sufficiently definite to be carried into effect. 

Harrison's Estate, 196 Pa. 576. The testatrix left a legally probated will but after her decease there was found an envelope containing five bonds and four stock certificates. 

On the envelope was this indorsement: "June 21, 1897. Six bonds for my brother John's three daughters, also one for my nephew John Beard, to be sold after my death. P. H. P. Harrison."

Similar legacies were given in the will to the same legatees. Held that the indorsement on the envelope was a valid codicil to the will and that the securities were properly awarded to the persons named in addition to the legacies given them under the terms of the will. 

In Coulter v. Shelmadine, 204 Pa. 120, a husband conveyed all his right, title and interest in certain land to his wife "her heirs and assigns, for her sole benefit and use during her natural life. After her death the same to be divided

among my legal heirs. Provided this assignment shall not be of any effect until after my death.' This paper was held to be testamentary in character and the wife did not take a fee simple in the lands. 

In Megary's Estate, 206 Pa. 260, the facts were that Sarah 

Megary signed a paper directed to "to whom it may concern" and stating that as a certain person mentioned therein had lived with her and had done various kinds of work and had made no charges for the same, it was the desire of the said Sarah that this person should receive a certain sum of money out of the said Sarah's estate. There was also an expression that this was not to affect any provision that she, the said Sarah, might make for this same person in "any will or testament" that the said Sarah might make.

It was held, reversing the decree of the Register and the Court below that this paper was testamentary in character and should have been admitted to probate as the will of the said Sarah. 

In Willing's Estate, 212 Pa. 136, the testator sent a letter of instructions to his attorney respecting a codicil to his will. 

This letter was signed by the testator and a copy was made of it and enclosed in an envelope which was endorsed with the words "copy of codicil to my will." This endorsement was not signed and the attorney never prepared the codicil and refused so to do. When the testator learned of the attorney's refusal he remarked, "it does not make any difference, you have that paper and that is all right." This testimony was only supported by one witness and it was held that the letter to the attorney with the endorsement on the envelope and the testimony in question were not sufficient taken together to establish a valid codicil. 

Windolph v. Girard Trust Co., 245 Pa. 349. The case of 

Lines v. Lines was followed, the facts being that a wife had made a deed of trust of personalty under practically the same facts as Lines v. Lines, supra. It was held that under the present legislation in Pennsylvania a wife has the same power of disposal of her personal estate during coverture, that her husband has of his personal property, and she can create a valid trust of her separate personal estate by deed

of trust during her life without the joinder or consent of her husband.

The doctrine of Lines v. Lines and Windolph v. Girard 

Trust Co., supra, is that the deeds of trust, although to be effective in part after the death of the settlor, are not testamentary in character and further that as regards personal property they are valid dispositions and not in violation of marital rights. See also Weaver v. Welsh, 71 Pa. Super. Ct. 

184; Potter v. The Trust Co., 199 Pa. 360; Benkart v. The 

Trust Co., 269 Pa. 257 and Mandel v. Bron, 270 Pa. 566, for qualifications of the above doctrine. 

In McCune's Estate, 265 Pa. 523, the paper read as follows: "I want you, E. A. Kerr, to look after my property and if I don't sell it I will sign it over to you for taking care of me." It was held that the paper was not testamentary in character and being absolutely free from ambiguity on its face extrinsic evidence as to the maker's intention was inadmissible.

In Davis's Estate, 275 Pa. 126, the paper was in the form of a letter using the expressions "Shoul I dye in the near futur" certain things were to be done. The quoted language was held to render the letter testamentary in character. 

Said Sadler, J: "No facts were in dispute, and had a jury trial been had, the court necessarily would have instructed as to the legal effect of the words in question. It is not for a jury to speculate upon a possible intention of a testator, but for the Court to interpret the language which appears: Brown v. 

Brown, 6 Watts 54; Curty v. Monnin, 14 Pa. Super. Ct. 102.

Like determinations are found where, upon undisputed facts, the question of the reasonableness of delay in the performance of some obligation is involved, it being the duty of the Court to solve the difficulty as a matter of law: 

Leaming v. Wise, 73 Pa. 173; Wright v. General Carbonic 

Co., 271 Pa. 332." 

Says Simpson, J. in Kimmel's Estate, 278 Pa. 435: "It is equally clear that where, as here, the words "if enny thing hapens" condition the gift, they strongly support く​て​です

the idea of a testamentary intent; indeed they exactly state what is expressed in or must be implied from every will. 

True, if the particular contingency stated in a paper, as the condition upon which it shall become effective, has never in fact occurred, it will not be admitted to probate: Morrow's App., 116 Pa. 440; Forquer's Est., 216 Pa. 331. In the present case, however, it is clear the contingency, "if enny thing hapens," was still existing when testator died suddenly on the same day he wrote and mailed the letter; hence, the facts not being disputed, the question of testamentary intent was one of law for the Court: Davis's Est., 275 Pa. 126.” 

In Wolfe's Estate, 284 Pa. 169, the writing was as follows: "Harrisburg, Pa., July 16, 1921 

"CENTRAL TRUST COMPANY No. 

"My Executor "For his labor "Pay to the "order of........Merle H. Baker.. "Forty Seven Hundred... .$4700.00 .. Dollars "Wash. M. Wolfe."

This paper was held to be testamentary in character. 

See Knight's Estate, 8 D. & C. 621 which may be compared with Lambaert's Estate, 10 Pa. C. C. 10, and Lilley's Estate, 11 D. & C. 183 which may be compared with Pritchett's 

Estate, 9 Pa. C. C. 600.

EXTRINSIC EVIDENCE OF TESTAMENTARY INTENT 

Referring to page 127, and following, supra, in this volume, will be found a series of cases discussing the matter of extrinsic evidence in support of testamentary intent. 

Testamentary intent is a matter of law for the Court in all instances but if facts relied upon to show testamentary intent are in dispute the case will go to the jury upon proper instruction from the Court. 

Let us look at the several situations. A paper propounded as a will may be clear as to the testamentary intent, i. e., it is stated in the paper that it is a will. In this instance the

rule of res ipsa loquitur is applied and all that is necessary is to prove by two or more competent witnesses that the paper as propounded was signed by the alleged testator at the end thereof. The paper is then properly admitted to probate. On the other hand the terms of the paper may be equivocal. The signature is at the end thereof and is proved by the requisite number of witnesses but here the rule of res ipsa loquitur does not apply. The Court may be in some doubt as to whether this paper is testamentary in intent. Extrinsic evidence is offered and whatever doubt was in the mind of the Court is dispelled. This extrinsic evidence may be supplied by one or more witnesses and in conjunction with the proving of the signature of the alleged testator will be sufficient. 

Kisecker's Estate, 190 Pa. 476, Diehl's Estate, 11 Pa. Super. Ct. 293. 

Said Stewart, P. J. in Kisecker's Estate, supra: "This paper was written and executed by the maker ten years before her death. It was never delivered to any one, but remained to the end in her exclusive possession, not that it had not been forgotten and was overlooked, for, until four or five days before her death, she had kept it where she must frequently have seen it, and in the very place of all others where one in her situation would be most likely to keep a will, and least likely to keep a deed,-in her Bible. A very few days before her death, she directed an attendant to read it aloud in her hearing and then to place it carefully away in some other place. To no one did she speak of it as her will, yet her retaining it in her possession in the manner she did, having it read over to her within a few days of her death, and then directing that it be put away in some safe place, such circumstances point unmistakably to the conclusion that she herself regarded it as a posthumous disposition of her property."

The Supreme Court affirmed the decree of the Lower Court ordering the Register to admit the paper to probate. 

Diehl's Estate, supra, arose in the same County Court and was affirmed by the Superior Court shortly after the

Kisecker case.

In the Diehl case the facts were that a paper was offered for probate containing, inter alia, these words: "I have given (not bequeathed) six hundred dollars or more, if necessary, to put a good iron fence around the graveyard near the Lutheran Church in this place. 

I wish the fence to be put up just as soon as the money can be collected for to have it put there. This is my wish." 

This paper was duly signed and the Court refused an issue d. v. n. Said Rice, P. J.: "This is not a case where no testamentary intent is apparent on the face of the instrument, and where it must be proven exclusively by extrinsic evidence. In such cases, the authorities seem to hold that two witnesses are necessary, each of whom must separately depose to all facts necessary, to complete the chain of evidence, so that if only one witness were required the will would be fully proved by the testimony of either. That rule does not apply, certainly not in all its strictness, to a case where a testamentary intent is entirely consistent with the language of the paper fairly construed in the light of the facts as to its execution and preservation. This is well shown in the opinion of Judge Stewart, approved by the Supreme Court in Kisecker's Estate."

In a dissenting opinion, Porter, J. observed: "I can find nothing in the case, save the testimony of one or more witnesses who say that the decedent referred to the paper as a will and the fact that the paper was found in the decedent's possession, to support the view that the document was in purpose testamentary." 

If the facts are in dispute the Court will send the case to the Jury and in such instances the disputed facts must be proved by the requisite number of witnesses according to the terms of the Wills Act and in conformance with the cases already cited previously at page 127, and following in this volume. 

See also Davis's Estate, 275 Pa. at page 130, per Sadler, J.

Assuming that the facts are in dispute must those disputed

facts arise out of the paper and its phraseology or may the facts be entirely extrinsic. 

For example in Sunday's Estate, 167 Pa. 30, the decedent executed seven judgment notes. There was nothing on these notes to indicate that they were other than ordinary judgment notes but after the decedent's death it was sought to prove that these notes were to be considered as a part of the decedent's will. Only one witness could be produced to testify to such facts and it was held that the evidence was insufficient to establish the testamentary character of the notes and consequently their probate as codicils to testator's will was refused.

The comment on Sunday's Appeal and other cases as made by Simpson, J. in O'Connor's Estate, 273 Pa. at page 

394, is as follows: "It is of course true that if a document offered for probate is testamentary in character, is executed in the manner provided by statute, and its purpose is that the whole or any part of the estate of the maker is to be given, after his death, to the distributees named therein, it is in law a will and may be probated as such, though in form a deed or contract: Turner v. Scott, 51 Pa. 126; Coulter v. Shelmadine, 204 Pa. 120. It is equally true, however, that in determining whether or not a paper, in form a deed or agreement, is testamentary and therefore entitled to probate, certain rules, founded in common sense and adopted by the law, have been steadily applied by the Courts. Thus it is said in the opinion of the Court below in Sunday's Est., 167 Pa. 30, 36, approved by this Court: "Where a decedent has done two acts, one of which is distinctively testamentary in form, and the other and later act is as distinctly nontestamentary in form, and is couched, with strict technical propriety, in the apt language of contract, there is no reason for holding the latter testamentary, without clear proof of fraud, accident, or mistake." So also we said in Fellbush v. Fellbush, 216 Pa. 141, 143: "Since the distinction in purpose between a deed and a will is so obvious and so generally understood, the fact that the form of one has been adopted rather than the other, is a circumstance which in some cases

くぐ ​may be of large significance. What the case of Turner v. 

Scott, supra, is authority for is that, where the language used in the instrument to express the purpose admits of but one construction, or has definite legal import, such outside and collateral inquiries have no place in the investigation for the reason that, in such cases, it is not a question of what the party may have meant or intended, but what is the meaning of the words he used." See instructive note on general subject, 12 Ann. Cas. 287, with comments on Pennsylvania cases.

DISCUSSION 

From the aforegoing cases in this chapter the following propositions are drawn: (1) A will may be written with any material and upon any material but the nature of the materials and the position of the testator at the time of execution will throw considerable light on the testamentary intent. (2) A will may be in any form of language provided testamentary intent can be construed therefrom. (3) The ascertainment of testamentary intent is a matter of interpretation of language and a question of law for the Court. (4) Where the language is not clear the Court may be aided in the interpretation by extrinsic evidence, in which case the two witnesses requirement is not applicable and circumstances disclosed may resolve any doubt existing as to the nature of the instrument. (5) If the Court determines as a matter of law that the evidence for the contestant or proponent would not support a verdict for either as the case might be, there are no grounds for the granting of an issue d. v. n. (6) If the Court determines that an issue should be granted or that the facts presented to the Court as the trier of the same raise a doubt, this doubt must be dispelled by the two witness requirements.

(7) If the language of the paper propounded is susceptible of but one meaning, there is no question of interpretation and extrinsic evidence is inadmissible. (8) Where the language of the paper is clear, the subscriber is bound by the legal intent deduced therefrom except in cases of fraud, accident or mistake.
