So stood the English law in 1705, when the legislature, in fulfillment of the fourth section of the charter to William Penn, directed the governor to appoint a register-general with an office fixed in Philadelphia, and direction to constitute a deputy with the like powers in each county. This pretty close imitation of the English plan continued in use, with few alterations or additions, till March 1777, when, in accordance with the thirty-fourth section of the constitution of the preceding year (repeated article five, section eleven of the present constitution) the legislature abolished the office of register-general, and directed a register to be appointed in each county, to be subordinate to no other of the class and so stands the matter at the present day. The jurisdiction of this officer is, of course, restricted to the county; but as only one administration is grantable anywhere, the authority derived from this power extends, by necessary consequence, over the state."

Scott, on the Intestate Law of Pennsylvania, at page 6, states: "Mr. Hood states, that the oldest book in the office of the Register of Wills at Philadelphia commences with the record of the will of Thomas Fream, which appears to have been proved on the tenth of the eight month, 1682. At that time, he observes, the title of Register General belonged to the officer who granted letters testamentary and of administration at Philadelphia. This title, and the power of appointing deputy registers in the other counties, belonged, down to the Revolution, to the Register at Philadelphia, his functions being modified and regulated by the acts of 1705 and 1712, which were supplied by the act of March 14, 1777. 

The office of Register General was abolished by the thirtyfourth section of the constitution of 1776, which provided for establishing a register's office in each county of the State,

www vesting the appointment in the General Assembly. The constitution of 1790 vested the appointment of Registers in the Governor. The present constitution provides that Registers of Wills shall be elected by the qualified electors of each county, for a term of three years, and be commissioned by the Governor."

The Commission of 1830 codified the law pertaining to the Register's office as we have it in the Act of March 15, 1832, P. L. 135; an act consisting of 45 sections and treating of 

Registers and Registers Courts. 

By the provisions of Article 5, Section 22 of the Con stitution of Pennsylvania, adopted in 1873, it was stipulated that in every county Orphans Courts shall possess all the powers and jurisdiction of a Register's Court, and therefore separate Register's Courts have been abolished, all reference to the same in the statutes having application now to the Orphans Courts.

The law on the subject was again codified by the Commission appointed in 1915 and the present law is embodied in the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 415, consisting of 26 sections. 

Section 3 of the Act of 1917 provides as follows: 

"Every Register qualified to act, as aforesaid, shall have jurisdiction, within the county for which he shall have been elected or appointed, of the probate of wills and testamentary papers, of the granting of letters testamentary and of administration, of the passing and filing of the accounts of executors and administrators, and of any other matter whereof the jurisdiction may be at any time expressly annexed to his said office; and the act of any Register, in any matter whereof another Register has the exclusive jurisdiction shall be void and of no effect." 

The above language is substantially that of Section 5 of the Act of March 15, 1832.

Section 4 of the Act of 1917 provides as follows: 

"Wills shall be probated only before the Register of Wills of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent, at the time of his decease, and, if the decedent has no such residence in this Common-

PROBATE 

339 wealth, then only before the Register of the county where the principal part of the goods and estate of such decedent within this Commonwealth shall be."

Section 2 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447 provides as follows: 

"Letters testamentary and of administration shall be grantable only by the Register of Wills of the county within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent, at the time of his decease; and if the decedent had no such residence in this Commonwealth, then ancillary letters testamentary or of administration shall be grantable only by the Register of the county where the principal part of the goods and estate of such decedent within this 

Commonwealth shall be.”

By the terms of Article 14, Section 2 of the present constitution as amended by vote of the people November 2, 1909, county officers, including Registers of Wills, beginning with the first Monday of January, 1910, hold office for the term of four years instead of three years as heretofore. 

The Act of June 29, 1923, P. L. 944, changes the compensation of Registers in counties of the sixth class from the fee basis to that of an annual salary of $3,000.00 and the act of July 11, 1923, P. L. 1054, makes a similar change for the Registers in counties of the fifth class, giving instead of fees a salary of $5,000.00.

For further statutory details in the matter of the office of Register of Wills, either as a separate office or combined with other county offices, pursuant to special acts of assembly and the position of Register of Wills as exofficio clerk of the Orphans' Court in counties where there is a separate Orphans Court judiciary see generally Purdon's Pennsylvania Statutes Annotated.

JURISDICTIONAL FACTS 

In order to establish the jurisdiction of the Register of Wills in the matter of probate proceedings, three facts must be ascertained and determined. First, the death of the testator, second, his residence, and third, his property, whether

personal or real, and its location. These jurisdictional facts will, therefore, be discussed in the order named. DEATH

The fact of death is obviously essential to the jurisdiction of the Register of Wills as well as the Orphans Court. As far back as 1824 we find the Supreme Court emphasizing this matter in the case of McPherson v. Cunliff, 11 S. & R. 

422, and in the well known case of Devlin v. Commonwealth, 101 Pa. 273, the action of the Register was deemed void because there was no actual fact of death of the person whose estate was in course of administration and it was pointed out therein that if the Register finds the fact of death erroneously, this being shown he is without jurisdiction.

This essential jurisdictional fact may be shown in any one of three ways. (a) By the testimony of those who actually saw the person die or attended his funeral or in some other direct way ascertained the fact of death. This is the most ordinary method of proving the fact and in the petitions for probate in the Register's Office there are appropriate blanks to be filled out giving the exact time and place of death to be subscribed under oath by those familiar with the facts. 

Another method of proving the fact of death (b) is by the testimony of witnesses giving evidence from which the inference of death may be drawn, a form of what is known as circumstantial evidence, viz., the alleged decedent was last seen in a burning building which was totally destroyed and he did not subsequently return to his usual haunts or his effects are found at the end of a pier extending into the ocean together with a note in the person's handwriting stating that he intended to destroy himself and he has not subsequently appeared at accustomed places. These and many other circumstances may be imagined which if presented as evidence to the Register may justify him in finding the fact of death and probating the will as offered. 

Another method of proving the fact (c) is by relying upon the presumption of death after seven years unexplained

PROBATE 

341 absence. The English rule is that in case of the absence of a person unexplained, the presumption of the continuance of life ceases at the end of seven years. This presumption has been transposed into the presumption of death after the expiration of the seven year period. 

In 3 Harvard Law Review, at page 154, Professor James 

Bradley Thayer, in an article entitled "Presumptions and the Law of Evidence", traces the origin of the presumption question, and among other things, states: "But the judges as well as text-writers got to expressing what had been put as a cessation of a presumption of life in the form of an affirmative presumption of death; and this was put as a rule of general application wherever life and death were in question. And so Stephen puts it. “A person shown not to have been heard of for seven years by those (if any) who if he had been alive would naturally have heard of him, is presumed to be dead, unless the circumstances of the case are such as to account for his not being heard of without assuming his death." This rule is set down by Stephen among the few presumptions which he thinks should find a place in the law of evidence; his definition of the term "presumption" being, as it will be remembered, "a rule of law that courts and judges shall draw a particular inference from a particular fact or from particular evidence unless and until the truth of such inference is disproved." Stephen published his Digest in 

1876. Here, then, in seventy years, we find the rule about a seven years' absence (1) coming into existence in the form of a judicial declaration about what may or may not fairly be inferred by a jury in the exercise of their logical faculty, the particular period being fixed by reference to two legislative determinations in specific cases of a like question; (2) passing into the form of an affirmative “rule of law" requiring that death be assumed under the given circumstances. This is a process of judicial legislation, advancing from a mere recognition of a step in legal reasoning to a declaration of the legal effect of certain facts. 

In Pennsylvania it is possible to put the finger on the very case that accomplishes this legislative stroke: the case

of Burr v. Sim, 4 Whart. 150 (1839). In 1817 (citing Miller v. Beates, 2 S. & R. 490) the court had laid down the duty of a jury to presume death, without any positive proof of it, when an unexplained absence for many years is shown; but they refused to adopt a seven years' rule. "I am not", said 

Tilghman, C. J., "for fixing any precise period after which a presumption of death rises. But here fourteen years and nine months," etc. In Burr v. Sim, however, the court (Gibson, C. J.) adopted the English rule, although in Pennsylvania there were no statutes like those in England; and they said: "If there is no direct decision, as there is in some of our States, it is because there has been no case requiring it. There is such a case now, and the principle is to be considered as definitely settled." In some States this rule, or the like, has been fixed by statute; but it is no less well established in others where it rests not upon a statute, but a judicial determination."

As has been stated Burr v. Sim, 4 Whart. 150, starts the beginning of the presumption of death doctrine in Pennsylvania. It is further exemplified in Whiteside's Appeal, 23 Pa. 114, and Campbell v. Reed, 24 Pa. 498.

In Appeal of Esterly, 109 Pa. 222, the facts were that A. was last heard of in May, 1870, when he disappeared from home leaving his wife and four children. His father died intestate in March of 1879. This disappearance of A. for 

7 years unexplained raised a presumption of his death and this presumption was as effective as direct proof of the fact. 

Consequently, as A. was presumed to be dead at the time of his father's death his share of his father's estate went directly to his children and heirs and the creditors of A. could not, therefore, participate in the distribution of this share.

In Schoneman's Appeal, 174 Pa. 1, in an action by the widow against a benefit association for death benefits it was held that the husband was presumed to be alive until the expiration of the seven years and that the presumption of death consequently would not begin to run until the limitation of the presumption of life.

PROBATE 

343 In Francis v. Francis, 180 Pa. 644, Thomas Watkins left the vicinity in which he was living in Pennsylvania for Patagonia, South America, in 1876, the purpose being to establish a colony in South America. Watkins was a member of this colony but had not been heard from since 1876, and it was contended that the presumption of his death would date from a time prior to 1884. Said Williams, J.: referring to the presumption: "Absence in this connection means that a person is not at the place of his domicile, and that his actual residence is unknown. It is for this reason that his existence is doubtful, and that after seven years of such absence his death is presumed. But removal alone is not enough. .. But where a person removes from his domicile in this state to establish a home for himself in another state or country, at a place well-known, this is a change of residence and absence from the last domicile is that upon which the presumption must be built." 

In McCausland's Estate, 213 Pa. 189, the ruling of Burr v. Sim was applied in this wise: 

A married man disappeared and was not heard of for seven years. During the seven year period his wife remarried and in a question concerning the legitimacy of a child by this marriage the court determined that although there was no proof of the actual date of the death and there was no presumption as to the time when during the seven years the death of the person disappearing actually occurred, nevertheless, as there was a presumption in favor of legitimacy and in favor of the validity of the second marriage the latter would be presumed as not occurring until subsequent to the death of the absent husband. Said Brown, J.: “Though seven years must elapse before the presumption of death arises, when this period does elapse there is no presumption as to the time when, during the seven years, the death of the absent party actually occurred, and, therefore, to help the presumption of innocence or legitimacy, there is no presumption that it occurred after the second marriage but rather that it occurred before."

In Baker v. The Trust Company, 55 Pa. Super. Ct. 15, referring to the McCausland case, Henderson, J. said: "This was a statement in another form of the rule that the presumption is in favor of legitimacy and of the validity of the second marriage as not having occurred prior to the death of the absent husband. One presumption encountered another; the presumption of the validity of the marriage overcame the presumption of the continuance of life of the man who had disappeared. This was not intended, however, to impair the force of the principle established in the cases cited or to disturb the titles resting thereon." 

Accordingly, where a son had disappeared and his absence unaccounted for, for less than seven years before the death of his mother, it was held that he would be presumed to have lived until after the death of his mother, and if the latter died intestate and the son also left no will and no children, the widow of the son would be entitled to a half interest for life in the real estate which descended to her husband and the income should be paid to her directly without the raising of an administration on her husband's estate. 

In Freeman's Estate, 227 Pa. 154, the son of a decedent had been absent and unheard of for more than seven years after his father's death, but there was evidence that he had been heard of within three or four years prior to his father's death. Held, that a finding of the Orphans Court that the son survived the father will not be reversed. In such a case the son's share of the personal estate of his father may be distributed directly to the personal representative of his mother. 

In Commonwealth v. Powell, 256 Pa. 470, Brown, C. J. quoted with approval the following from Chamberlayne on the Modern Law of Evidence, Volume 2, section 1117: 

"Any fact which fairly and reasonably tends to rebut the inference assumed to be correct in the presumption of death is admissible. For example, it may be shown by the opponent that the absentee had a motive for his silence, as that he was a fugitive from justice, had absconded from his

PROBATE 

345 creditors, or has some other reason for concealing his identity. So one who has run away from an orphan asylum, prison, jail or other places of involuntary detention, will not be inferred or assumed to be dead from the same facts which might fairly ground the inference or assumption in case of one with less inducement to conceal his whereabouts."

In Maley v. The Railroad Co., 258 Pa. 73, it was stated that where the absentee's possible destination was known when he left, reasonable search should be made at the place where he was last known to live before the presumption of death can arise. Where death is found by a Court of Common Pleas having jurisdiction of the subject matter involved, said fact of death being upon the presumption raised by the absence of a person unheard of for seven years and by reason of such death money from a benefit association becomes due, the contention of defendant that it might be compelled to pay again if the presumption of death were subsequently overthrown is without merit as the defendant is properly protected by the judgment of the court.

In Groner v. Knights of Maccabees, 265 Pa. 129, a wife brought an action in the Common Pleas Court against defendants for the recovery of insurance on the life of her husband whose death was alleged through the presumption. 

The facts were that the husband, after leaving his wife and home, did not take up any permanent residence elsewhere but roved from place to place and had no settled or established domicile except the one which he had first abandoned. 

The wife had made several diligent efforts to find his whereabouts by inquiry and by advertisement offering reward, and the present suit was brought more than seven years after last hearing from him. In sustaining a verdict and judgment for plaintiff in the sum of $2,000.00, Moschzisker, J., before the court, delivered an opinion which beginning at page 133 and extending to page 136, reviews the leading cases in Pennsylvania on the subject of death by presumption.

In Roblin v. Knights of Maccabees, 269 Pa. 139, a certificate of membership in a fraternal order was issued to 

William Roblin in 1889. Thereafter Roblin removed with his family to Pittsburgh and in 1902 he left his home and was not heard of since. In 1918 the Orphans Court of Allegheny County, after due proceedings, decreed the presumption of his death and directed the appointment of an administrator of his estate. All dues and assessments were paid by Roblin until his disappearance and afterwards by his wife till after the decree of the Orphans Court when she surrendered the certificate to defendant and brought this suit for the death benefit named therein. A verdict and judgment were rendered for the plaintiff in the sum of $2,220.00 and the judgment was affirmed by the Supreme 

Court, citing the former case of Groner v. the Knights of 

Maccabees, 265 Pa. 129.

In Jaskalski v. Catholic Union, 64 Pa. Super. Ct. 535, a wife took two of her four children, aged five and six years respectively, and abandoned her husband. Nine years after the desertion of his wife the husband became a member of the defendant association and designated as beneficiaries "his children”. Two years thereafter one of the two children who remained with the husband died, and later the husband died twenty-two years after the desertion of his wife, leaving surviving a daughter. The latter brought suit against the beneficial association for the death benefits, and it was held that she was entitled to rely on the presumption that the two children who had been taken away by their mother were dead at the time of the trial of the case. Said the court, per Orlady, P. J., after reviewing the leading cases in Pennsylvania on the subject of disappearance: "The time here, twenty-five years, is sufficient to establish the presumption of death as to the mother, or either of the children, and no reason is suggested why it should apply to one and not to the others. 

While there are exceptional cases exempting children from the force of the presumption when they accompany parents, it can only reasonably apply while they remain in a dependent condi-

PROBATE 

347 tion, and when they reach or approach maturity they must become subject to the general rule, and in this record, Mary and Julia had been unheard of for more than nineteen years after each attained her majority."

In Young v. Sweigart, 69 Pa. Super. Ct. 525, a son disappeared in 1875 and his mother died intestate in 1880. The presumption of life continued until the expiration of seven years, hence the son was presumed to be alive in 1880 and he would take as an heir under the intestate laws. 

In O'Hara v. The Insurance Co., 73 Pa. Super. Ct. 434, A. was a resident of the City of Philadelphia and on or about the 28th of June, 1907, disappeared from his home and since that date neither the plaintiff, his wife, nor the other members of his family have heard from him. Said Henderson, J., referring to the facts: "Evidence tending to establish the fact that the insured was seen in Atlantic City August 15, 1911 would not be a good answer in an action begun September 24, 1918 where a presumption of death was alleged because the insured had not been heard from for more than seven years." 

In Elliott v. Insurance Co., 76 Pa. Super. Ct. 534, the insured left his home in Philadelphia October 2, 1909 to take a position as a strikebreaker in Newcastle, Pa. Upon arrival there he sent word to his wife by postal and by letters, the letters being received on October 17, 1909, and from that date he never afterwards was heard from, although his wife caused advertisements to be inserted in newspapers in Pittsburgh and in Newcastle, together with inquiries made through the labor union of which he was a member, and the wife herself went to Chicago and spent a considerable length of time there endeavoring to obtain some tidings of her husband. Defendant, in an action brought upon the policy, made no serious attempt to contradict this testimony. Said Porter, J.: "The evidence was certainly sufficient to warrant a finding that the insured had been absent and unheard of for seven years, that period expiring on October 17, 1916. The presumption of death arising from an unaccounted absence

of a person for seven years must be taken to run exclusively from the termination of the prescribed period, so that the person must be taken to have then been dead, and not before: Baker v. Fidelity Title and Trust Company, 55 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 15; O'Hara v. Metropolitan Life Insurance Co., 73 Pa. Super. Ct. 434. The presumption that the insured was dead, if evidence produced by the plaintiff was true, as the jury found it to be, arose with the expiration of the day, October 17, 1916."

For a case attempting to apply the presumption of death to a claim under the Workmen's Compensation Act, see Condron v. The Railroad Company, 78 Pa. Super. Ct. 133 and for a case holding that in an action of assumpsit on a life insurance policy the decree of the Orphans Court, assuming its admissibility in such a case, was not conclusive proof of the death of the absentee, under the Fiduciaries 

Act of 1917, Volmer v. The Insurance Company, 101 Pa. 

Super. Ct. 117.

Compare the latter case with Maley v. The Railroad Company, supra.

For a recent case involving the conflicting presumptions of death and innocence in a marriage case, see Feustal v. 

Krul, 8 D. & C. 369.

In Trust of Levering, et al, 9 D. & C. 328, it was said that in the absence of proof that a person was confronted with any peril that might reasonably be expected to destroy his life, or that he was in any particular or immediate danger, it will be presumed that he lived until the expiration of seven years from the time he was last heard of and that his death occurred at the end of the seventh year. 

For the cognate subject of death in common disaster and the application of the common law rule of no presumption, as to which died first, see 

Sweeney's Estate, 78 Pa. Super. Ct. 417. 

Cordes's Estate, 3 D. & C. 551. 

Baldus v. Jeremias, 296 Pa. 313.

See also on this general subject, 14 Harvard Law Review 

538, and 16 Harvard Law Review 368.

PROBATE 

349 Presumption of death has also been made the subject of statutory enactment by the terms of which the Orphans Court have been specifically empowered. This legislation was first enacted in the provisions of the Act of June 24, 1885, P. L. 155 in response to the case of Devlin v. Commonwealth, 101 Pa. 273, decided by the Supreme Court of 

Pennsylvania three years before. The present law is found in the Fiduciaries Act of 1917. 

Section 6 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of 1917, P. L. 447, provides as follows: "Whenever, hereafter, any person shall be presumed to be dead, on account of absence for seven or more years from the place of his or her last domicile, whether the same be within this Commonwealth, or in any other state, territory or possession of the United States, or in any foreign country, any person entitled under the last will and testament of such presumed decedent or under the intestate laws to any share in his or her estate within this Commonwealth, or the escheator for the Commonwealth, may present a petition to the Orphans Court of the county of such person's last residence or, where the presumed decedent was a non-resident of this Commonwealth, in the Orphans Court of the county where the greater part of his property within this Commonwealth may be situated, setting forth the facts which raise the presumption of death. 

The said court, if satisfied as to the person who would be entitled to letters testamentary or of administration were the presumed decedent in fact dead, shall cause to be advertised, in a newspaper published in said county, once a week for four successive weeks, together with such other advertisement as the court, according to the circumstances of the case, shall deem expedient or advisable, the fact of such application, together with notice that on a day certain, which shall be at least two weeks after the last appearance of said advertisement, the court, or master appointed by the court for that purpose, will hear evidence concerning the alleged absence of the presumed decedent, and the circumstances and duration thereof."

Section 6, as above partially quoted, contains nine para-

graphs from a to n inclusive, paragraph (b) provides for the issuance of letters ancillary on the estate of a presumed decedent. The other paragraphs take care of the various phases in the procedure incident to the grant of letters, probate of wills, and administration of such estate. Said Hull, Deputy Attorney-General in In Re Inheritance Tax of persons presumed to be dead, 1 D. & C. 502: "Section 6 of the Fiduciaries Act provides the procedure to be followed in the case of one presumed to be dead. 

After presentation of a proper petition to the Orphans Court and advertisement of notice, a time for hearing is fixed. At the hearing, if the legal presumption of death is made out, the court frames its decree and determines therein the date when the presumption of death arose. Notice of this decree is then published, and a period of twelve weeks must elapse after the date of the last publication, within which time, if satisfactory evidence be produced that the presumed decedent is still alive, the decree will be vacated. 

If such evidence is not forthcoming, then the decree theretofore made is confirmed absolutely, and the court thereupon directs the Register of Wills to issue letters of administration, etc. to the person entitled thereto." 

These provisions embody, inter alia, the Act of 24th of 

June, 1885, P. L. 155, the Act of April 14, 1905, P. L. 153, and the Act of May 28, 1913, P. L. 373.

Section 6 (a) supra, was amended by the Act of April 27, 1927, P. L. 425, as follows: "Whenever, hereafter, any person shall be presumed to be dead on account of absence for seven or more years from the place of his or her last domicile, whether the same be within this Commonwealth or in any other State, Territory, or possession of the United States, or in any foreign country, any person entitled, under the last will and testament of such presumed decedent or under the intestate laws to any share in his or her estate within this Commonwealth, or under any deed, will, or other instrument in writing, or in any other way, method, or manner, to any share or interest in any estate held by or for such presumed decedent, for years or for the term of his or her natural life, or the

PROBATE 

351 escheator for the Commonwealth, may present a petition to the Orphans Court of the county of such person's last residence, or, where the presumed decedent was a non-resident of this Commonwealth, in the Orphans Court of the county where the greater part of his property within this Commonwealth may be situated, setting forth the facts which raise the presumption of death. The said court, if satisfied as to the (person who would be entitled to letters testamentary or of administration were the presumed decedent in fact dead shall) interest of the petitioner, may cause to be advertised in a newspaper published in said county, once a week for four successive weeks, together with such other advertisement as the court, according to the circumstances of the case, shall deem expedient or advisable, the fact of such application, together with notice that, on a day certain which shall be at least two weeks after the last appearance of said advertisement, the court, or master appointed by the court for that purpose, will hear evidence concerning the alleged absence of the presumed decedent and the circumstances and duration thereof. 

Section 2. This act shall apply to all proceedings pending at the date of its passage."

For the history and constitutionality of Section 6, supra, see the following cases: 

Devlin v. Commonwealth, 101 Pa. 273.

Scott v. McNeal, 14 Sup. Ct. Rep. 1108; Cunnius v. Reading School Dist., 21 Pa. Super. Ct. 340, 206 Pa. 469, 25 Sup.

RESIDENCE Section 4 of the Register of Wills Act, June 7, 1917, P. L. 

415, provides as follows: "Wills shall be probated only before the register of wills of the county within which was the family or principal

residence of the decedent at the time of his decease; and, if the decedent has no such residence in this Commonwealth, then only before the register of the county where the principal part of the goods and estate of such decedent within this Commonwealth shall be."

This section is modeled and complementary to Section 2 (a) of the Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447. See for these Acts, 20 P. S. Sections 341 and 1862. 

The language of Section 2 (a) supra, is similar to that of 

Section 6 of the Act of March 15, 1832, P. L. 136. 

Said Clayton, P. J., in Lewis's Estate, 10 Pa. C. C. 331, in referring to the Act of 1832: "The Act of Assembly when it uses the word "residence" means the same thing as is expressed by the common law in the word "domicile". A man's domicile is always chosen by himself. The mere fact that he may dwell in a certain place for, comparatively, a long time does not make that place his domicile unless he intended it to be such. His intention is to be gathered from his words and conduct." 

On the other hand, in Blessing's Estate, 29 D. R. 3, affirmed 267 Pa. 380, Gest, J. declared: "It may be admitted that in some of the decisions the words "residence" and "domicile" are used as synonymous but, strictly, in cases of administration, succession, etc. the law of domicile applies when questions arise as to the application of a law of different states, or of this state, and that of a foreign country."

Referring particularly to the words of Section 2 (a) of the Fiduciaries Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 447, the learned court states: "The Act clearly refers to residence, not domicile; it says, "the family or principal residence". A man can have but one domicile, though he may have any number of residences, therefore, his "family or principal residence" in this conflict between two counties as to the jurisdiction of the register of Wills, must mean the place where he actually resides with his family, and this was undoubtedly in Glenside."

PROBATE 

353 In Taney's Appeal, 97 Pa. 74, counsel for the appellee used this argument: "The vice of the appellant's argument is in confusing the terms "domicile" and "residence", and treating them as synonymous. A man may be a resident of one place while he is domiciled in another, and a man whose domicile is Pennsylvania may be a non-resident of that state, even though he has not acquired a residence elsewhere. 

The distinction between "domicile" and "residence" is a clear one, and if adhered to will harmonize many apparently conflicting authorities. Residence, as distinguished from domicile, has been defined to be "a personal presence, without any present intention to depart." ...... 

In Raymond v. Leishman, 243 Pa. 64, on a foreign attachment issued against the property of John G. A. Leishman at the time Ambassador of the United States to Germany, the question was whether the defendant was a person residing within this Commonwealth at the time of the issuance of the writ within the meaning of the Act of March 30, 1905, P. L. 76, authorizing the issuance of a foreign attachment against the real or personal estate of any person not residing within this Commonwealth and not being within the county in which such writ shall issue at the time of the issuing thereof. 

The Supreme Court in holding that the writ would lie, stated, inter alia, as follows, per Mestrezat, J.: "It is clear that "residence" and "domicile" are not convertible terms, and that the latter is of more extensive signification. While these principles are well settled, it is also true that as used in many statutes, "domicile" and "residence" have been held to be equivalent terms. The courts have so construed statutes relating to the qualification of voters, to homesteads, to taxation, to the statute of limitations, to succession, guardianship, and administration, and in those prescribing the jurisdictional prerequisites to the maintenance of actions for divorce or separation. 

It is, therefore, apparent, and the courts have held that "residence" is a word whose statutory meaning depends upon the context and the purpose of the statute, which may, 12

as used in one statute, be fulfilled by mere business residence, and in another require domicile in the strictest and most technical sense. In ascertaining the meaning of the word "residence", in a particular statute the Legislative purpose, as well as the context, must be kept in view." 

See also, 14 Cyc. 835; 34 Cyc. 1647.

In the Century Dictionary, "domicile" is defined as follows: 

"The place where a person has his home, or his principal home, or where he has his family residence and personal place of business; that residence from which there is no present intention to remove, or to which there is a general intention to return."

It is apparent that the Legislature, in specifying the locality "within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent at the time of his decease", has referred to that permanent residence which is a part of the definition of domicile.

One can have but a single domicile, but he may have several residences, as a town residence and a country residence or a residence in Pennsylvania and another residence in Florida, or one residence in Adams County and another residence in Franklin County. 

The requirement of the statute is that the principal or family residence shall constitute the proper location for the grant of probate on the estate of one who was at the time of his death domiciled in Pennsylvania.

The cases in Pennsylvania discussing the subject of domicile have, therefore, a relevancy in this discussion and may aid us in determining the facts essential to "the family or principal residence." 

In the early report of 1 Binney, at page 349, note, two cases are recorded discussing the question of domicile, namely, Desesbats v. Berquier and Guier v. O'Daniel. 

Said Rush, P. J.: "A man is prima facie domiciled at the place where he is a resident at the time of his death, and it is incumbent on those who deny it to repel this presumption of law. ... ......

PROBATE 

355 There is no fixed period of time necessary to create a domicile. It may be acquired after the shortest residence under certain circumstances and under others the longest residence may be insufficient for the purpose." 

There are two domiciles known as the domicile of origin or birth, and the domicile of choice. The question is one of fact to be determined by the circumstances of each case. 

Said Lewis, J., in Hood's Estate, 21 Pa. 106: "We have said that the domicile of origin continues until it is changed by acquiring one elsewhere. But where a person removes to a foreign country, settles himself there and engages in the trade of the country, the presumption in favor of the continuance of the domicile of origin no longer exists, and the burden of disproving the domicile of choice is cast upon him who denies it. That the domicile of origin was abandoned in this case admits of no doubt whatever. The decedent's long residence in Cuba, under circumstances indicating an intention to remain there, sufficiently fixes his permanent domicile in that island. His investments in this country, and the interest he had in a mercantile house here, can work no change in his place of abode. His occasional visits, on business or pleasure, to the land of his birth, have as little effect upon the question. His desire to be buried in his native country, and the execution of that wish by his executor after his death in France, whither he had gone for medical aid, cannot change the state of the case as it actually existed in his lifetime. residence is established by acts and intentions while the body and soul are united. When they are separated, the question of domicile is at an end. No disposition of the inanimate corpse can affect it. Graves and sepulchres are resting places for the dead, not dwelling houses for the living."

In Harberger's Estate, 8 W. N. C. 470, the question was before the Register of Wills on the probate of a will, whether the residence of the testatrix was in Lancaster or in Philadelphia, and the court in passing upon an appeal from the decision of the Register, said, inter alia:

"After a careful examination of the evidence, there can be no doubt that the "principal residence" of the decedent within the meaning of the act of assembly was at Lancaster, Pa. This is gathered from her acts and declarations during the period of the last seven years of her life, and they all show that she left her residence in that city with the intention of returning, that she was detained away longer than she had anticipated by visiting her sons, the care and oversight of the property in this city in which she had a life estate, and by sickness and the infirmities of old age, which prevented her from travelling alone. During all this time she continually referred to Lancaster as her home, upon frequent occasions expressed her desire to return, and not a single witness was called to show any contrary intention, not even the appellee himself. And in addition by numerous letters to her sons this same intention is manifested and wish reiterated." 

In Carey's Appeal, 75 Pa. 201, testator made a will in

Pennsylvania, witnessed by two witnesses, but the evidence showed that his domicile was in Rhode Island where three witnesses are required. It was held, therefore, that probate of the Pennsylvania will by the Register in Philadelphia, should be revoked and the letters testamentary vacated. Said Gordon, J.: "Two things must concur to constitute domicile-first, residence; secondly, the intention of making the place of residence the home of the party. There must be both fact and intent. So, though the residence be taken for temporary purpose, intention may change its character to a domicile, but prima facie the place of residence is the domicile until other facts establish the contrary. Even a recent establishment was held to constitute a domicile where the intention of making it a personal residence was proved upon the party."

In Hindman's Appeal, 85 Pa. 466, the evidence showed that George Hindman was born in Brooke County, West Virginia, where he resided till 1869. Then he moved on a farm which he had purchased in Hancock County of the

PROBATE 

357 same state. There he resided until March 1871. He then sold his farm, which was all the real estate he owned, and went to live with his brother-in-law, McClurg, in Washington County, Pennsylvania. He never married, and had no family. His property was all in personal estate. He took with him his horse, a box containing his notes, bonds and valuable papers. Soon afterwards he brought his other horse to McClurg's, leaving in West Virginia only some farming implements of little value. He continued to live with 

McClurg paying his board and made his home there until April, 1872. He then went to live with Gibson, another brother-in-law, in Washington County, Pennsylvania, taking with him his box, bureau, and table. There he continued to live until his death 22 June, 1872. Said Mercur, J.: "When he sold the farm on which he had lived, he gave up possession and removed therefrom. He thereby gave up that domicile. He then made no new abode, and established no other residence in that state. He gathered up his property, and with it departed and located in another state. 

This unequivocal act of moving from the state and taking up his residence in another state, is very strong evidence of the establishment of a domicile in the latter. Its effect is not destroyed by his expressed and indefinite intention to go back into West Virginia at some future time and there buy land. Nothing less than a present intention to retain his domicile there would prevent its transfer to the state into which he moved. He did not come into Pennsylvania for his health or as a traveler, nor for any other particular business of a temporary nature." 

Accordingly, the decree of the Lower Court, holding that the domicile of the decedent was in West Virginia was reversed and record remanded. 

In Kirby v. Bradford County, 134 Pa. 109, a bill in equity was filed by Kirby against the Commissioners of Bradford County to set aside an assessment and to restrain the collection of taxes upon personalty on the ground that the plaintiff was a non-resident of the state. The master found that the plaintiff had been a resident of Bradford County from the age of twenty-three until the age of

sixty-eight, which age he attained in 1885. In the previous year he made visits to California and spent his winters in that state, but always returned to Bradford County at which times he stated that he intended to take up his residence in California, but during his absence from Pennsylvania he left his family in Bradford County, paid their expenses and continued the ownership of a residence or dwelling until the time of the taking of the testimony in this case, which was in March, 1889. In 1887 he voted in California, but paid no taxes there except upon a mortgage he held upon property owned by his son-in-law. 

Upon the foregoing facts and others of like character, the master held that the plaintiff's residence or domicile was in Towanda Township, Bradford County, on and prior to January 3, 1887. The decree entered by the Lower Court was affirmed on appeal. 

In Price v. Price, 156 Pa. 617, the facts were that the testator's domicile of origin was West Chester, Pennsylvania; that his domicile of choice was Brooklyn, New York; that, having purchased a farm near West Chester, he returned from Brooklyn to West Chester, where he died. 

It was held that under the pleadings the burden of proof was on plaintiff to establish a change of domicile and that it was not error for the court to charge that if the jury conclude that testator abandoned his residence in Brooklyn with the intention of residing on his farm, or in Philadelphia, but died before consummating that intention, Brooklyn continued to be his legal place of residence. Said Sterrett, C. J.: "In the absence of affirmative proof to the contrary, the presumption would be that Brooklyn continued to be the place of his legal residence until his decease. The defendant was certainly not required to prove a negative especially in view of the pleadings in which, as we have seen, the plaintiff assumed the burden of proving the affirmative facts upon which his whole case depended." 

Barclay's Estate, 259 Pa. 401, accord.

In Dalrymple's Estate, 215 Pa. 367, it was held on an appeal from a collateral tax assessment in the estate of Dalrymple that where a person died in a town where he had

PROBATE 

359 lived, and owned real and personal property, had voted, and had a personal tax, had been deemed to have been domiciled at such town at the time of his death, although he had been frequently away from it, owned property in other states, and had declared that he expected to make his home in a city in another state. Said Mestrezat, J.: "The authority of the Orphans Court to determine the domicile of the testator, notwithstanding the action of the probate court of Milwaukee County, Wisconsin, in admitting his will to probate and granting letters testamentary, is clearly sustained by the numerous authorities cited in the opinion of the court below."

In Bertch's Estate, 45 Pa. C. C. 642, there was an appeal from the decree of the Register of Wills of Erie County admitting to probate the will of Adam Bertch. Said Whittelsey, J, after reviewing numerous decisions on the subject of domicile: "From these decisions it would appear to follow that the legal residence and domicile of Adam Bertch at the time of his death was in the County of Lancaster and not in the County of Erie. He was not a tax payer in the County of 

Erie. He had no family residing therein and never had. He was not a voter in said county and never had been. He was simply an inmate of the Pennsylvania Soldiers and Sailors Home at the City of Erie and kept there at the expense of the State of Pennsylvania. As said by Judge Walling in the decision above referred to (21 Pa. C. C. 473), his relations were with the home and not with the city of Erie. 

On the other hand, it appears that he had for many years prior to his becoming an inmate of the home been a resident and property owner and tax payer in the County of Lancaster, and presumably a voter, and had his domicile therein, and under the decision of Judge Walling, in 21 Pa. 

C. C. 443, he still had the right to vote in Lancaster County, if otherwise qualified. We cannot, therefore, escape the conclusion that the Register of Wills in Lancaster County, the domicile of the testator, has jurisdiction over the probate of the will of the said Adam Bertch, and the proceedings had before the Register of Wills of Erie County, and all sub-

sequent proceedings should be set aside and that the records and papers in the case should be certified to the Register of Wills of Lancaster County for him to take such action as he may deem advisable in the probate of the will in question, and that the costs in this proceeding should be paid out of the money in court belonging to the estate of the said 

Adam Bertch, deceased."

As has already been indicated in previous discussions if the subject matter of probate was within the general jurisdiction of the Register the decree is conclusive and cannot be questioned collaterally. For example, the Register of one county having found the fact of residence of decedent to have been in his county and having, therefore, probated the will, the Register of another county cannot set aside the probate upon the ground that the decedent was a non-resident of the first county. 

Shoenberger's Estate, 27 W. N. C. 129. 

Harberger's Will, 13 Phila. 368.

PROPERTY 

Where the decedent was a resident of Pennsylvania, as we have seen, his will is probated before the Register of the County "within which was the family or principal residence of the decedent at the time of his decease." This particular Register alone has jurisdiction to probate the will. On the other hand according to the provisions of Sec tion 4 of the Register of Wills Act of June 7, 1917, P. L. 415 

"if the decedent has no such residence in this Commonwealth, then only before the Register of the County where the principal part of the goods or estate of such decedent within this Commonwealth shall be."

In other words, where the testator did not reside at the time of his decease in Pennsylvania, but left property located in Pennsylvania, the will of such decedent shall be probated in that County wherein lies the principal part of the goods and estate of such decedent. The total amount of the estate is not calculated but the total amount which lies within the borders of Pennsylvania and then the County

PROBATE 

361 wherein lies the principal part of such goods so located in the State. 

In Shoenberger's Estate, 139 Pa. 132, 27 W. N. C. 129, the testator died a resident of New York City, leaving an estate located in New York, Pennsylvania, and elsewhere. His will was probated in New York and an exemplification of the record was later presented to the Register of Wills of Philadelphia County and letters ancillary were granted to the executors named therein as to the estate in Pennsylvania. 

Later the Register of Wills of Allegheny County conceiv ing that the letters were improvidently granted in Philadelphia County, issued a citation to the executors to show cause why they should not appear before him and take out letters in Allegheny County, and after hearing testimony he decreed that letters would issue to them upon their applying for that purpose within ten days and upon failure, letters with the will annexed would be issued to some other fit person. The executors appealed from this decree to the 

Orphans Court of Allegheny County, which court affirmed the decree of the Register, hence this appeal. Said Paxson, C. J.: 

"When application was made to the Register of Wills of Philadelphia, he had a right to inquire as to where the principal part of the goods and estate of the testator were situate in this state. It was a jurisdictional question which it was his duty, as well as his right, to decide. He therefore had jurisdiction over the subject matter, and his decision cannot be set aside collaterally as void. The learned judge lays much stress upon the fact that there is no averment or finding in the records of the proceedings before the Register of Philadelphia County, that the principal part of the estate was in it. But it is begging the question to assume that he did not pass upon it. The 5th section of the Act of 1832 contains no provision that the Register shall preserve the evidence upon which he acts, and we are bound to presume, as in every case of a judicial officer, that he has done his duty. While his decision stands unappealed from, it is conclusive, and cannot be reversed and set aside by the decision of the Register of another county."

See also 

Cook's Estate, 27 D. R. 1006. 

Frick's Appeal, 114 Pa. 29.

Sayre's Exrs. v. Helme's Exr., 61 Pa. 299. 

PROBATE PROCEDURE 

The probate of a will and the taking out of letters testamentary, as well as the grant of letters of administration by the Register of Wills, are all events preceded by a petition directed to the Register praying that the wills be probated and the letters issued. Prior to the passage of the 

Fiduciaries Act the practice throughout the state was by no means uniform. In Philadelphia and Allegheny Counties a written petition embodying the facts duly signed and sworn to was required, but in most of the counties very little formality was observed in connection with these matters, and usually the applicant appeared in the office of the Register and by parol made known his request to have letters granted. If there was any opposition to the granting of letters, or the probate of the will, it was generally made known to the Register in the shape of a caveat, in which case the Register issued a citation to the parties interested to appear upon a day named and to show cause why the prayer of the petitioner should not be granted. Upon the return day testimony was taken and arguments presented, and after due consideration the Register handed down his decision. On the other hand, if no opposition was manifest and the facts appeared to be plain as represented to the Register ex parte, letters of administration or the probate of the will, or both, would follow as a matter of course. 

In these counties the only record which was kept of the issuance of letters consisted of the oath taken by the administrator to well and truly perform the duties of his office according to law, together with the affidavit of a third person setting forth the time and place of death of the person upon whose estate letters were prayed for, and finally the entry of the decree of the Register setting forth that upon a certain day letters of administration were in due

PROBATE 

363 form of law granted to the petitioner in the estate of the particular deceased person. 

By the terms of Section 2 (d) of the Fiduciaries Act of 

1917, P. L.

447, the procedure was made uniform throughout the state. The paragraph is as follows: 

"Every application to any Register of wills for the issuance of letters testamentary or of administration shall be in the form of a petitioner, duly verified by affidavit, setting forth the residence and citizenship and the place, day and hour of the death of the decedent, the estimated value of his property, real and personal, the location of his real property, and, in the case of an intestacy, the names and residences of the surviving spouse, if any, and of the next of kin of the intestate, together with an averment that the persons named are the surviving spouse and all the next of kin of the intestate."

This paragraph has been amended by the Act of March 

24, 1921, P. L. 51, by the addition of this sentence: "In the case of applications for letters testamentary, such applications shall set forth whether the testator has married and whether any children have been born to such testator since the execution of the will offered for probate." 

In Sharpless's Estate, 28 D. R. 746, Harman, P. J. after quoting section 2, clause d, observed: "This proviso is mandatory and the wisdom of the enactment is well illustrated in the present instance. Had it been complied with, all of this litigation would have been avoided and costs saved, to say nothing of delay. From the record and from the testimony, uncontradicted, the fact is established that no petition was filed at the time of the granting of these letters. And the act of the register in granting letters without this petition, even with or without misrepresentation as to the facts of the estate, was an error, not of discretion, but of power. This appeal brings up the whole record, and where it appears to us that the letters issued to the appellants in this case were issued without compliance with the mandatory requirements of the Act of Assembly in such case made and provided, we have the right to take

cognizance thereof and act accordingly. See Winklefoose's 

Estate, 5 York Leg. Rec. 151."

It is to be noted that the statutes do not provide for the filing of a petition setting forth the facts as required in Section 2 (d) supra, where merely the probate of the will is desired. Consequently, the loose practice prevailing in some of the counties prior to 1917 relative to the issuance of. letters and probating of wills still continues in the one aspect of probating of wills without the issuance of letters. 

This is a serious defect and should be remedied by amendment as the registers being judicial officers cannot be compelled to follow any particular procedure unless by command of the statute law. It is an elementary principle that the Register of Wills is a judicial officer of a court not of record and as such is a separate and independent county officer whose duties are prescribed by statute. 

Topham's Estate, 12 D. R. 4, 20 P. S. Section 1861, Note 1. 

Furthermore, the register is not required to swear witnesses or to reduce to writing the testimony heard by him or to state in writing the reasons for his decision or to preserve for transmission to the Orphans Court upon appeal, the testimony taken by him. 

Failor's Estate, 10 Pa. Super. Ct. 253. 

Furthermore, he is apparently not amenable to rules of practice as they may be promulgated by the Orphans Court. 

Topham's Estate, supra, See generally, 20 P. S. Section 1861, Note. CAVEAT 

Says Scott on the Intestate Law, at page 20: "Caveat, let him beware, is a notice given by a party having an interest, to some officer not to do an act till the party giving the notice has a chance to be heard; as, to the 

Register of Wills not to permit a will to be proved, or not to grant letters of administration; or to the land officers not to give a patent; or to a clerk in chancery not to enroll a decree until the objections can be heard. It always precedes the act, and is never heard of as a means of undoing what has already been done."

PROBATE 

365 

Section 20 of the Register of Wills Act of 1917, P. L. 415, provides as follows: "It shall not be lawful for any register of wills, having jurisdiction of the probate of wills and the granting of letters testamentary and of administration within this Commonwealth to entertain, consider or regard any caveat against the probate of any last will and testament, or the granting of letters testamentary or of administration, or any appeal from the probate of any such will, or from the grant of any letters testamentary or of administration, unless such caveator or caveators, appellant or appellants, shall, within ten days after the filing of such caveat or appeal, enter into a bond, in the name of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, with at least two sufficient sureties to be approved by the register, in a penal sum of not less than five hundred dollars, and not to exceed five thousand dollars, as may be determined by the said register, conditioned for the payment of all or any costs which may be occasioned by reason of such caveat or appeal, and which may be decreed by such register or by the Orphans Court to be paid by such caveator or appellant, which bond shall remain on file in the office of such register. 

In case no bond, such as aforesaid, shall be filed with the register within ten days after the filing of any caveat or appeal, as aforesaid, such caveat or appeal shall be considered as abandoned, and shall be dismissed, and proceedings may be had in all respects as if no such caveat or appeal had been filed."

Upon the filing of a caveat this action inures to the benefit of all parties interested. 

Phillip's Estate, 293 Pa. 351.

The Register may, accordingly, issue a precept to the 

Common Pleas for an issue d. v. n.

Section 17 of the Register of Wills, Act, supra, provides for this procedure in the following terms: "Whenever a caveat shall be entered against the admission of any testamentary writing to probate, and the person entering the same shall allege as the ground thereof any

matter of fact touching the validity of such writing, it shall be lawful for the register, at the request of any person interested, to issue a precept to the Court of Common Pleas of the respective county, directing an issue to be formed upon the said fact or facts, and also upon such others as may be lawfully objected to the said writing, in substantially the following form, viz: (L. S.) . County, ss:

The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, To the judges of the Court of Common Pleas of the said county, Greeting: 

Whereas, A. B., on the......day of....in the year, et cetera, presented to G. H., our register of wills of said county, for probate a certain writing, hereto annexed, purporting to have been made the........day of......, in the year et cetera (or otherwise describing the paper in question), which said writing the said A. B. avers is the last will and testament of the said C. D.; and whereas E. D., who is a son and heir of the said C. D. (or intermarried with F. D., who is a daughter and heir, et cetera, according to the fact), hath objected before our said register that the said writing was procured by duress and constraint (stating the matters of fact objected); and whereas, the said A. B. (or E. D.) hath requested that an issue may be directed into our said court to try by a jury the validity of the said writing, and the matters of fact which may be objected thereto in our said court: therefore, we command you that you cause an action to be entered upon the records of our said court, as of the day of the delivery of this our precept into the office of the prothonotary of our said court, between the said A. B. and the said E. D., so that an issue therein may be formed upon the merits of the controversy between the said parties, and tried in due course according to the practice of our said courts in actions commenced by writ: and further that you cause all other persons who may be interested in the estate of the said C. D., as heirs, relations, or next of kin, devisees, legatees, or executors, to be warned, so that they may come into our said court and become party to the said action, if they shall see cause; and that you

PROBATE 

367 certify the result of the trial so had in the premises into the office of our said register. 

Attest: G. H., Register of Wills of the said county.

And the facts established by the trial, had, and certified to the register as aforesaid, shall not be re-examined by the said register, nor upon any appeal from his decision." 

It will be observed that first the section does not require the register to direct an issue but the matter is discretionary on his part. 

Wikoff's Appeal, 15 Pa. 281. 

Graham's Appeal, 61 Pa. 43. 

Commonwealth v. Bunn, 71 Pa. 405.

And on the other hand the register cannot frame an issue except "at the request of any person interested." 

Fow's Estate, 27 W. N. C. 373.

Furthermore, the mere filing of a caveat will not justify the action of the register in framing an issue for the person entering the caveat "shall allege as the ground thereof any matter of fact touching the validity of such writing". Many caveats are framed in general language simply notifying the register not to grant letters or probate a will as the case may be until the caveator is given an opportunity to be heard.

The usual practice is to make the proponents plaintiffs in the issue and those who object to the will as defendants. 

Ruddach v. Reichenbach, 1 Pa. C. C. 500. 

Carter's Estate, 2 D. R. 578.

For valuable note on this general subject see 20 P. S. 

Section 1961. 

Another angle of the register's powers and limitations is found in Section 18 of the Register of Wills Act, supra, which provides as follows: "Where a caveat is entered against the probate of any last will or testamentary paper, or where there is a dispute as to such probate or as to the granting of letters testamentary or of administration, the Orphans Court of the county in

which said will or testamentary paper has been offered for probate or said letters testamentary or of administration have been applied for, may, by general rule or by special order in the case, on the petition of the register of wills of said county or of any party interested, direct said register to certify the entire record thereto pertaining to said court, which shall then determine whether the will or testamentary paper shall be admitted to probate or an issue devisavit vel non be directed to the court of common pleas of said county, or whether said letters testamentary or of administration shall be granted, in like manner as if the said will or testamentary paper had been admitted to probate, or said letters testamentary or of administration had been granted, by said register and an appeal been taken to the Orphans Court from his decree. The record may be thus certified at any stage of the proceedings before the register, and after its removal to the Orphans Court no letters of administration pendente lite shall be granted by the register except by leave of the Orphans Court on cause shown by any party interested." 

The draftsman of this Act has stated that the section just quoted is new and intended to prevent the needless and sometimes intentional delays which have often occurred in the prosecution of proceedings before registers. 

In Henry's Estate, 30 D. R. 945, it was held that upon petition made to the Orphans Court and an order issued to the Register to certify the entire record of proceedings in accordance with Section 18, that thereupon the Register's jurisdiction over the matters before him ended and that letters of administration pendente lite granted pursuant to an appointment made by him before the service of the order are void and should be vacated by the court. 

In Griffiths' Estate, 276 Pa. 277, there was a rule to remit record of Register of Wills, a petition having been presented to the Orphans Court pursuant to the provisions of Section 18, and a date for a hearing was fixed. After notice of the action of the court and without taking any evidence, the Register acted favorably upon a caveat filed and sent the will to the court of Common Pleas with his

PROBATE 

369 precept directing an issue to be there formed to determine whether or not the will was valid, pursuant to the provis ions of Section 17 of the Register of Wills Act of 1917. Upon the case reaching the Supreme Court, Simpson, J. inter alia, said: "This action by one who is Clerk of the Orphans Court (Constitution of Penna. Art. 5, Sec. 22), which prevented him from obeying its order, if it subsequently granted the prayer of the petition would (if he was intentionally flouting the court's authority, which we have no reason to believe) have been perilously near, if it was not actually, a contempt of court.”

Said the learned justice further, referring to the pro visions of Section 18: 

"This power in the Orphans Court to take the record away from the Register necessarily carries with it a suspension of his power, while yet unexercised, whenever, he has had notice that the court is considering whether or not it will so order in the particular case; and wholly defeats that power if the court concludes to decide the question itself."

The question referred to in the last quotation was whether an issue would be awarded as suggested in Section 17. 

To this case an appeal was taken after the Register had acted under the terms of Section 21 (a) of the Register of Wills Act of 1917, and the learned justice commenting on this procedure stated: "So, also, when the register has acted, and has granted an issue to the common pleas, section 21 (a) provides that, 'appeals may be taken to the Orphans Court,' from 'all decisions granting an issue devisavit vel non;' and hence, when such an appeal is taken, this wholly defeats the prior action of the register in granting the issue." 

See generally the opinion of Simpson, J. in Griffiths'

Estate, supra, for explanation of the co-ordination of Sections 17, 18 and 21 (a) of the Register of Wills Act of June 

7, 1917, P. L. 415.

In Cranmer's Estate, 3 D. & C. 369, it was held that where

the contestant makes out a strong case and there is evidence, which, if taken alone, is sufficient to support his allegations, but there is also sufficient evidence in support of the validity of the will, if believed by a jury, to sustain a verdict in its favor, the Register cannot properly refuse to issue his precept to Common Pleas and peremptorily refuse probate. 

Section 19 of the Register of Wills Act of June 7, 1917, 

P. L. 415, provides as follows: "Where objections are made, or a caveat is entered, against the probate of any last will and testament, and no precept for an issue is directed by the register into the Court of Common Pleas as aforesaid, or where objections are made to the granting of letters testamentary or of administration to any person applying therefor, or where any question of kindred or other disputable and difficult matter comes into controversy before any register, he may certify the entire record thereto pertaining to the Orphans Court of the county, for the determination by said court of such disputable and difficult matter, giving convenient notice of the time when the matter will be heard in said court to all persons interested."

The draftsman of the Commission has appended to this section the following note: 

"Note. This is founded on Section 25 of the Act of March 

15, 1832, 4 Purd. 4081, which provided for the appointment of a register's court to determine such matters. It has been held that the section was not repealed by the abolition of Register's courts by the constitution of 1874, and that such matters are now to be certified to the Orphans Court: Com. v. Clark, 1 W. N. C. 330. The section has been revised accordingly.

The draft, instead of providing that the register "shall, at the request of any person interested, certify the entire record," etc., provides that the register may certify the record and omits the provision as to request by a person interested. The last preceding section of the draft provides a method for the compulsory removal of the record, and it seems best to make the certification under the present section discretionary with the register.

In Commonwealth, ex rel, v. Allen, 33 Pa. C. C. 88, a writ of mandamus was prayed for to compel the register of wills to certify to the Orphans Court contested proceedings pending before him on the probate of an alleged will under the provisions of Section 25 of the Act of March 15, 1832, P. 

L. 142, and it was held where the evidence taken before the register of wills on the probate of a will shows that a disputable question has arisen as to whether the decedent had physical or mental capacity to make a will, or whether undue influence has been exercised upon him, the register is bound to certify the disputable question to the Orphans Court and if he refuses to do so he may be compelled by mandamus. 

In 20 P. S. Section 1982, Note 5, it is said: "Section 25 of act 1832, March 15, P. L. 135 (repealed) is mandatory; and when the matter is plainly disputable, the register has no discretion as to certifying or not certifying the subject to the Orphans Court.
